715.title: Bhishma's vow
715.howItsDone: Some Hindus remember Bhishma on a day called Bhishma Ashtami, offering water in his name, a rite usually made for one's own ancestors, since he left no children to make it for him.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Bhishma's vow: one word, mother, a chariot ride to Hastinapura, and the kings saying, he is truly Bhishma. Who did you tell what they mean to you? Day seven hundred fifteen.

Shantanu has just heard everything his son did at the fisherman's house: the throne given away, the lifelong vow, the bride brought home and called mother. Bhishma asked for nothing in return. He only told his father what he had done. Now his father gives him something anyway, and it's rare: a say over his own death. Death will not come to you, the king tells him, in the text's sense, as long as you wish to live.
screen: `A GIFT FROM FATHER TO SON.` → `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` → `DEATH ONLY WITH HIS LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The text says Shantanu was pleased by the hard thing his son had done. And he gives him a boon: death will never approach you while you want to live. It will come only when you give it leave. Tradition calls this icchamrityu, death at will. Look at the shape of the exchange. The son gave away his future: a crown, a marriage, children of his own. The father answers with power over the one thing no one usually gets to choose: the end of his own life. A man who has given up the next generation is given the right to decide how long his own will run. And reach back once more. When Vasishtha softened his curse, he said the Vasu who took the cow would live long on earth. Now the long life is in Bhishma's own hands. That's the last piece of Bhishma's vow, and it's a good place to let the story breathe, because readers have taken this vow more than one way. In some retellings and in some homes, Bhishma's vow is held up as devotion to a father, a son putting his parent's happiness above his own. Some readers have asked harder questions: about a king who let his son pay that price for his own wish, and about how much one promise should bind a life. The Mahabharata doesn't settle it here. It gives us the vow, the flowers, the name, the word mother, and the boon, and then it moves on to the bride herself. Her story begins long before this marriage.
screen: `THE KING IS PLEASED.` · `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE ALLOWS IT.` · `HE GAVE AWAY HIS FUTURE.` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `THE LONG LIFE IN HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: Let the body be still, and simply watch the breath. Notice where each breath begins, and where it ends. You don't decide its length. It arrives, it rests, it goes. Follow one breath all the way in and all the way out, then another. If your mind runs ahead, come back to the edge of the breath you're on. Stay with beginnings and endings, gently, for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's vow. A son's promise to his father, answered with a father's boon: death will come to him only with his leave.
Your line: Bhishma's vow. Today, thank someone out loud for something they gave up for you. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Satyavati
716.howItsDone: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Bhishma's vow: a father's boon, death only with his son's leave. Who did you thank for something they gave up for you? Day seven hundred sixteen.
screen: `THE LONG LIFE IN HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell. He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river. This is where Satyavati's story begins.
screen: `A HAWK OVER THE YAMUNA.` → `A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.` → `IT FALLS INTO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls. Some time later, fishermen catch her, and when they cut her open, they find two human children inside, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends; she rises from the fish's body and goes back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king. And the king makes a choice. He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be a king named Matsya. The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen. Let her be your daughter, he says. She grows up beautiful, and she carries the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati. Now go back to the riverbank, a few days ago in our reading, when Shantanu asked who she was. I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she told him. Every word of that is true. The man who raised her is her father. But she's also a king's daughter, born from an apsara's body, handed away as a baby while her brother stayed in the palace. The poem gave us that half long ago, in its account of the ancestors, before she ever set foot in a boat. The fisherman who bargained so hard for her son's crown was bargaining for the child a king gave away. A king's daughter, a fisherman's child, rowing travelers across a river. She'll be a queen of the Kurus. But that's not where she started. Tomorrow we stay with her a little longer, before the palace, out on the river with her boat.
screen: `ADRIKA, THE CURSED APSARA.` · `TWINS FOUND IN A FISH.` · `THE KING KEEPS THE BOY.` · `LET HER BE YOUR DAUGHTER.` · then, large: `A KING'S DAUGHTER, A FISHERMAN'S CHILD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, the way a boat settles when the oars rest. Bring to mind the people who raised you, or who stood in for the ones who couldn't: a parent, a grandparent, a foster parent, an aunt, a coach, a neighbor. Let them be as they are, with all their halves. Breathe in, and notice where you came from. Breathe out, and notice the people who took you in along the way. Both are part of the story. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A king's daughter found in a fish, given away as a baby, and raised as the fisherman's own.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, ask someone you know well where they started, and listen to the whole answer. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Satyavati
717.hook: a sage steps into a fisher girl's boat on the Yamuna, a mist comes down, and she asks for one thing
717.howItsDone: Vyasa is honored as a teacher in Hindu tradition, and some Hindus keep the full moon called Guru Purnima, also known as Vyasa Purnima, as a day to thank their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday we met Satyavati, the fisherman's daughter who will one day be a queen of the Kurus. Whose story of where they started did you hear? Day seven hundred seventeen.

Before the palace, there's a boat. Satyavati rows travelers across the Yamuna for her father, the chief of the fishermen. It's ordinary work, and the river is wide. One day a sage on a pilgrimage steps in and sits down. His name is Parashara. Out on the water, he looks at her, and he wants her. And the young woman holding the oar has to think fast, alone, in the middle of a river. What she says next is where today's story turns.
screen: `A FERRY ON THE YAMUNA.` → `A SAGE STEPS IN.` → `OUT ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The Adi Parva gives Satyavati words here, and she uses them carefully. There are sages on the banks, she tells him. They can see us. So Parashara makes a mist, and the banks disappear. Then she names her next worry. I'm a maiden, she says, living under my father. What becomes of me afterward? Parashara answers that she'll remain a maiden. And then he tells her to ask for something for herself. Out of everything she could ask, she asks for one thing. Her body has carried the smell of fish since the day she was found inside one. She asks that it smell sweet instead. He grants it. From then on, the text says, people knew her by her fragrance, and it carried a long way across the land. On an island in the Yamuna, she gives birth to a son. With his mother's leave, he goes off to the forest to practice austerities. But before he goes, he leaves her a promise: whenever you think of me, I'll come. The text says he was called Dvaipayana because he was born on an island. Tradition knows him as Vyasa, the one the Mahabharata is credited to, whose disciple told it at Janamejaya's sacrifice. So hold two things from this boat. The fragrance: years from now, the scent that draws King Shantanu to a riverbank was asked for here. And the promise: think of me, and I'll come. Satyavati keeps that promise to herself for a long time. Some readers see a girl bargaining with the little power she's given. Some see a woman caught in a sage's power, asking for what she can. The text doesn't settle it. It just lets her ask.
screen: `THE BANKS ARE WATCHING.` · `A MIST COMES DOWN.` · `ONE THING, FOR HERSELF.` · `A SON BORN ON AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `THINK OF ME, AND I'LL COME.`

segments.voice: Find a steady seat and let the breath slow. Picture the river going quiet under a mist, the banks gone. Satyavati was offered one thing for herself, and she knew what it was. So try the question gently. If someone offered you one thing, not for your family, not for work, just for you, what would it be? Let the first answer come, and the second. Don't rush to the noble one. Breathe in with the question. Breathe out, and let it go quiet again. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. The ferry girl who asked for a fragrance, and kept a son's promise to herself.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, when someone offers you something, ask for the one thing you actually need. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Satyavati
718.hook: Satyavati's husband dies, her proud elder son meets a Gandharva who shares his name, and only one of them walks away
718.howItsDone: When a death comes in a Hindu family, the funeral rites are often led by a son or a close male relative, as Bhishma leads them for Chitrangada in the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat: a mist, a fragrance, and a son who promised to come whenever she thought of him. What one thing would you ask for? Day seven hundred eighteen.

Two warriors face each other, and they have the same name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians, a powerful one, the text says. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, we go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu, on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons: Chitrangada, and then Vichitravirya. And before the younger one is grown, Shantanu dies. So now Satyavati is a widow in a palace she came to from a river, with two boys, and a stepson, Bhishma, who has sworn never to take the throne. Bhishma keeps his word. He places Chitrangada on the throne, and he answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives. They fight on the field of Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, a long and bitter fight, and the Gandharva, with the tricks of his kind, kills the prince. Notice where the fight happens. Kurukshetra is a name this serial will come back to. Now notice what the text doesn't say. It gives the battle and the funeral rites, which Bhishma performs. It gives no speech from Satyavati. A woman who has lost a husband now loses a son, and the poem is quiet about her. Some readers fill that silence with grief. Some see her steadiness in what comes next, because Bhishma, with her, sets the younger boy, Vichitravirya, on the throne, still a child, and rules the kingdom for him. The house of the Kurus now rests on a boy king, a queen mother, and a stepson bound by a vow. Keep that picture. Everything this week grows out of it.
screen: `TWO SONS, AND A KING'S DEATH.` · `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `A QUEEN, A BOY, AND A VOW.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle into its own pace. Chitrangada believed no one was his equal, the text says, and a challenger came to test it. Bring to mind one thing you've had to win lately that didn't need winning: an argument, a small slight, a point of pride. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it. Breathe in, and notice how much effort the winning took. Breathe out, and let it rest where it is. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A widowed queen with one son lost to his namesake, and one boy left on the throne.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, let one small argument go without needing to win it. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: Satyavati
719.hook: Bhishma carries off three princesses for Satyavati's boy king, and the eldest tells the court her heart is already given
719.howItsDone: In the epics a swayamvara is a gathering where a princess chooses her husband from the suitors; Hindu weddings today come about in other ways, and the word is still known through these stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati lost her husband and her proud elder son, and a boy, Vichitravirya, was left on the throne. Which small argument did you let go? Day seven hundred nineteen.

Word reaches Hastinapura: the king of Kashi has three daughters, and they'll choose their husbands at a swayamvara, a self-choice, with kings gathered from everywhere. Vichitravirya has grown into a young man, and Bhishma has decided he should marry. So, with Satyavati's leave, Bhishma rides out alone in a single chariot to the city of Varanasi. He doesn't go there to be chosen. He goes there to take, and the whole court will watch him do it.
screen: `THREE PRINCESSES OF KASHI.` → `A SELF-CHOICE.` → `BHISHMA RIDES ALONE.`

segments.voice: Bhishma arrives, and the kings there laugh at the old man come courting. He answers by lifting the three princesses onto his chariot. Then, before them all, he names the ways a bride may be won, and says that a bride carried off by force is held in high regard by the wise. The kings take up their weapons, and he fights them, and defeats them, one after another, including the king of Saubha, named Shalva. Then he brings the three sisters home to Satyavati, as if they were his own daughters, the text says. It's a hard scene to hear today, and the text tells it without apology. Then the story turns. As the wedding is prepared, the eldest sister, Amba, speaks. She tells Bhishma that in her heart she had already chosen Shalva, and that he had chosen her. You know dharma, she says. Do what's right. And Bhishma, the man who just won her by force, stops. He consults the learned men of the court, and he lets her go to Shalva. Her story doesn't end there; the Mahabharata comes back to Amba much later, and we'll meet her again. The younger two, Ambika and Ambalika, marry Vichitravirya. And for a while, the text says, the young king is devoted to them and they to him. Then he falls ill with a wasting sickness, and despite his friends and his physicians, he dies, still young, with no son. And Satyavati, who has now outlived a husband and two sons, is left with a palace, two young widows, and a stepson who swore he'd never be king.
screen: `A SELF-CHOICE AT VARANASI.` · `CARRIED OFF BY FORCE.` · `AMBA SPEAKS.` · `A YOUNG KING DIES WITHOUT A SON.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the shoulders soften. In a room full of men who'd already decided her life, Amba said what was true for her. Bring to mind one thing you've left unsaid, because the decision seemed made already, or the room seemed too full. You don't have to say it now. Just let yourself know it clearly. Breathe in, and let the words form. Breathe out, and let them rest, ready. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A queen mother whose house gains two brides, lets one go, and loses its young king.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, when a decision about you seems already made, say one true thing about it anyway. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: Satyavati
720.hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he refuses her
720.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, offerings to the ancestors are called shraddha, and some families keep the season called Pitru Paksha for them; the worry in this story is that no one will be left to make them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati's house: three princesses carried from Kashi, Amba set free, and a young king dead without a son. What true thing did you say? Day seven hundred twenty.

A family line is a thin thread. Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. And the only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore, years ago, so that her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him to her. And the woman his vow was made for is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, the way someone does who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know what dharma asks. So do this: take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly. In the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her of what he swore, and why: so that her children would rule. And then he says something like this: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater than that, but he will not give up truth. The earth could lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. Hear how strange that is. The very vow that made her a queen is now the thing standing between her and an heir. Her father's condition drew that vow out once. Now she asks for it back, and it won't come back. Some readers see Bhishma's refusal as the poem's picture of keeping one's word at any cost. Some see it as the first sign that his vow will cost his family dearly. The text gives both of them room. Satyavati asks once more, for the need of the moment, and he still holds. But there's one thing she hasn't told anyone yet, and tomorrow she tells it.
screen: `THE ANCESTORS' OFFERINGS.` · `TAKE THE THRONE, SHE ASKS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.` · `THE VOW THAT MADE HER QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Settle in and let the breath find its own length. Bhishma's word held, even when the person it served asked him to drop it. Bring to mind one promise you're still keeping. It might be small: a weekly call, a debt, a habit you swore to. Hold it in mind without deciding anything about it. Ask it quietly: who is this still for? Breathe in on the promise. Breathe out on the people it touches. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. The queen who asks Bhishma to break the vow that made her queen, and hears him refuse.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, look at one promise you keep and ask who it's still for. Day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: Satyavati
721.hook: Satyavati finally tells Bhishma about the boat, the island and her firstborn, and calls Vyasa with a thought
721.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition Vyasa is honored as the sage who arranged the Vedas and composed the Mahabharata, and in this part of the poem he steps into the story he tells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati asked Bhishma to break his vow, and he would not give up truth. Who is your promise still for? Today ends the week. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He reminds her of old stories, of lines that were carried on in hard times when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none. Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells the stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.
screen: `FIND A LEARNED MAN.` → `SHE SMILES, AND FALTERS.` → `A SECRET FROM THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: She tells him about the boat. About the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island. She tells him that son is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and that when he left, he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, she says, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees. And Satyavati thinks of her son. That's all it takes. Vyasa appears, the text says, at once. He bows to his mother, and she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs. Now look back over the week. It began with a father's boon sealing Bhishma's vow, the vow that let a fisherman's daughter's sons rule. Then we went back to her beginning: a baby found in a fish, a boat, the fragrance she asked for, a son's promise. Then the losses came one by one: a husband, a proud son killed by his namesake, a young king dead of sickness. Three princesses were brought from Kashi, and Amba spoke and was let go. Then the queen asked Bhishma to take back his vow, and he wouldn't. And now, at the end, the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, in a boat on a river. A woman who started as a ferry girl has become the person holding the house of the Kurus together. Some readers see in her a schemer; some see a survivor; the text gives her its last word today: she remembers, and her son comes.
